question:
A 35-year-old man, with a history of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) diagnosed 2 years ago, presents with hearing loss in the right ear and tinnitus. Patient says that symptoms have been gradually progressive. He has difficulty hearing speech as well as loud sounds. He also gives a history of occasional headaches and vertigo on and off for 1 month, which is unresponsive to paracetamol. His vitals include: blood pressure 110/78 mm Hg, temperature 36.5°C (97.8°F), pulse 78/min and respiratory rate 11/min. Tuning fork tests reveal the following:
  Left Right
Rinne’s test  Air conduction > bone conduction  Air conduction > bone conduction
Weber test Lateralized to left ear 
Other physical examination findings are within normal limits. An MRI of the head is ordered which is as shown in image 1. A biopsy is done which shows cells staining positive for S100 but negative for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). The histopathological slide is shown in image 2. What is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) -> bilateral vestibular schwannomas -> hearing loss and tinnitus -> progressive symptoms -> difficulty hearing speech and loud sounds -> occasional headaches and vertigo -> unresponsive to paracetamol -> normal vital signs -> Rinne's test showing air conduction > bone conduction bilaterally -> Weber test lateralized to left ear -> MRI showing bilateral vestibular schwannomas -> biopsy positive for S100, negative for GFAP -> Most likely diagnosis: Schwannoma -> opc. Schwannoma -> 95%
enhanced_information: The patient's presentation of bilateral vestibular schwannomas, confirmed by MRI and biopsy findings, along with the clinical symptoms of hearing loss, tinnitus, headaches, and vertigo, align with the most likely diagnosis of Schwannoma (opc). The evidence paths related to Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein and other genes are not directly relevant to the diagnosis of Schwannoma in this context.
analysis: The patient's history of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), bilateral vestibular schwannomas confirmed by MRI and biopsy findings, along with the clinical symptoms of hearing loss, tinnitus, headaches, and vertigo, strongly suggest the most likely diagnosis of Schwannoma (opc). The positive staining for S100 in the biopsy further supports this diagnosis.
